newsitem.title: USA: IATA launches Cargo 2000 to speed air freight.
newsitem.headline: IATA launches Cargo 2000 to speed air freight.

text.p: Airlines and freight forwarders have launched IATA's Cargo Week 97 by charging a special task force called Cargo 2000 to develop recommendations on how to streamline the entire freight handling process, from shipper to consignee.
"This is certainly the biggest development in the industry in some time," says Colin Mills, director of cargo services for IATA (International Air Transport Association) told Reuters.
"It's the first time that forwarders and airlines have sat down together and said we must work together to improve this industry," he added.

Airlines and freight forwarders have paid enormous amount of lip service over the years to the need for closer cooperation in the face of the huge market share gains by integrated carriers like FedEx, industry sources said.
The continuing threat posed by integrators to the traditional IATA airlines and forwarders is one of the major reasons driving the Cargo 2000 process, said Mills.
Cutting out unnecessary duplication in processes and administrative practices will have broad implications for all of the players in the industry, he added.
"The forwarders and airlines will save by improved processes and lower costs, and the customer will gain with improved customer service, he said.
Initially, 27 airlines and forwarders have joined Cargo 2000, which IATA describe as a special interest group.

A great deal of its focus will be on duplication which occurs entirely within the jurisdiction of the carriers and forwarders - as opposed to areas like customs, which are government and regulatory issues, said Mills.

"The airlines and forwarders do an awful lot of double and treble and quadruple handling," he said, "They'll store cargo and they'll move it from one place to another place and then store it in another place. All these transactions build time and cost and inefficiencies. They (airlines and forwarders) are all saying we really have to have a close look at all this and cut it out. Let's make the process far more efficient, it needs to be far more efficient."

There is no government representation on Cargo 2000, and none will be sought, though the group is likely to identify areas where work has to be done in areas where there is a government involvement of some kind, he added.
It will not deal with security issues. It will look at implementing standards that already exist or developing new ones where needed.

Priority areas for the group will include certain EDI messages, such as: status messages, the electronic airway bill. There is a need to speed implementation of universal bar-coding standards, said Mills.
Where it believes that IATA standards should be amended or changed altogether, its recommendations will be brought into the formal IATA conference machinery, which will do so, he added.
At Sunday's inaugural meeting, the group named United Airlines cargo vice-president Jim Hartigan as chairman, with Klaus Geissler of Schenker International as vice-chairman.
An executive steering group who will refine the work plan.

The impetus for a joint initiative of airlines and forwarders came from an IATA cargo symposium last September in Paris, said Mills. Participants identified a need for process to help spur changes which all agreed were needed badly.

Cargo 2000 also builds on the work begun by the Cargo Media group, which has been wound up. Cargo Media, which would up its activities here Sunday, was exclusively an airline initiative. Cargo 2000 adds the involvement of forwarders.

Mills said that it is hoped that the steering group will have much of the studies and recommendations developed by September, at which time the full Cargo 2000 committee will probably meet again in Europe to consider them, said Mills. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax:5017
